No Titanic engineer survived the sinking.

When the RMS Titanic struck an iceberg on the night of April 14, 1912, Chief Engineer Joseph Bell and his 35-man team remained at work in the engine and boiler rooms. The crew included engineers, electricians, boilermakers, and a plumber.

As the ship flooded, they kept the engines running, the pumps pumping, and the lights on. Their efforts helped the wireless operators send distress calls and prevented the Titanic from plunging into darkness too soon.

None of them survived.

The entire engineering department was lost—a sacrifice often overlooked in accounts of the disaster. No one lived to describe the rising water, the failing machinery, or their determination to keep working until the very end.

They weren’t trying to save themselves. They were giving everyone else a chance.

Their courage kept the Titanic lit as it sank and its pumps running. Those final minutes gave hundreds of passengers more time to reach the lifeboats.

Altyn-Köl, Russia

Tucked beneath the snow-covered peaks of the Severny Chuysky Range in the Russian Altai, Altyn-Köl—“The Golden Lake”—shimmers in vivid shades of turquoise. Surrounded by glaciers and rugged mountains, it feels worlds away from the present.

Formed during the Ice Age, the lake gets its striking blue-green color from mineral-rich mountain waters. Here, silence stretches across the landscape, broken only by the wind, the cry of an eagle, and the old legends carried through the land.

More than a natural wonder, Altyn-Köl is woven into the heart of Altai culture, with its nomadic heritage, spiritual traditions, and Chaga-Bayram, the traditional New Year. Locals regard the lake as sacred—a mirror reflecting the bond between sky and spirit.
